newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ PM accused of treason, sabotage over economy.
newsitem.headline: NZ PM accused of treason, sabotage over economy.

text.p: Opposition leaders accused Prime Minister Jim Bolger of economic sabotage and treason on Monday after he encouraged foreign investors to take a cautious approach until the October 12 election.

Bolger, in danger of losing power to a trio of left and centre-left parties, was asked in an Australian television interview on Sunday what assurances he could offer investors who were worried by political uncertainty.

"I can only say that their uncertainty or their question mark at this stage two weeks out is totally understandable," he replied. If he was an Australian or overseas investor, Bolger said, he too would "just wait two weeks" to see if a sensible coalition emerged.

Bolger went further, saying no one was likely to invest in New Zealand if the left-wing Alliance was in the forefront of a coalition, and many New Zealanders would wish to ship out to Australia if that happened.
"Let me say to Australians, if we get some of the loopy policies of the left come in to New Zealand again, you will get a whole lot of Kiwis over there in a hurry," he said.
Opposition leaders expressed outrage over the remarks.
"What could be more irresponsible than to warn foreign investors not to invest in New Zealand before the general election?" Labour leader Helen Clark said in a statement.
She said the inference was that foreign investors should not only hold fire until the election, but should not invest if there was a change of government.

"Mr Bolger's message is no less than economic sabotage of his country ... what appals me is that Mr Bolger has cynically set out to destroy the New Zealand economy because the people of New Zealand are likely to judge him no longer fit to govern."

Winston Peters, leader of the economic nationalist New Zealand First party, attacked Bolger and the chairman of the country's biggest company, Telecom, for "bad mouthing" the New Zealand economy to Australian audiences.
"It's political treason...and could be economic treason were it not for the fact the Aussies are not as dumb as Jim Bolger," Peters told a public meeting.

"He is behaving like a spoilt brat. He is saying: 'I have to be prime minister or things will be disastrous'. Well, people are saying they are disastrous now and we don't want you to be prime minister".

Telecom chairman Peter Shirtcliffe told an Australian business audience earlier in the campaign that their NZ$20 billion (US$14 billion) in investments in New Zealand could be at risk if populist politicians gained power -- a clear reference to New Zealand First and the Alliance.

Latest polls show the election, New Zealand's first under proportional representation, is finely balanced. Bolger's conservatives are set to be the biggest single party but the leftist parties may muster a parliamentary majority.
